name: Penrose Tiling

lumenary.blurb: Two rhombus shapes that fill the plane without ever repeating, with five-fold symmetry that no ordinary tiling can have.

why: A tiling that repeats can be slid over itself and matched, but a Penrose tiling cannot. It never repeats and yet it is ordered, with five-fold symmetry that ordinary periodic tilings are forbidden to have. Two rhombus shapes are all it takes, and the golden ratio runs through every proportion in it.
how: Start with ten thin Robinson triangles arranged round the centre in a decagon.
Deflate every triangle: a thin one becomes two, a thick one becomes three, with new vertices placed along the old edges in the golden ratio.
Each round shrinks the edges by 1/φ and multiplies the number of triangles by about 2.618.
Look up the picture at the centroid of each triangle to find its colour.
Merge the triangle halves back into rhombi when drawing, with thick and thin tiles shaded in picture, two-tone or mixed mode.
history: The English mathematician and physicist Roger Penrose found these tilings in 1974, building on work by Robert Berger. In 1982 Dan Shechtman observed metal crystals with five-fold symmetry that should have been impossible, called quasicrystals, and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2011. Peter Lu and Paul Steinhardt argued in 2007 that medieval Islamic girih tilings came close to the same idea.
uses: Floor and wall design, such as paving at the Oxford Mathematical Institute
The study of quasicrystals in materials science
Cryptography and computer science research on tilings
terms: Never repeating, however far you look.
The number (1 + √5)/2, about 1.618, which appears in the proportions of the tiles.
A crystal with order but no repeating unit.
paragraphs: The Penrose tiling uses two rhombi, a thin one with angles of 36 and 144 degrees and a thick one with 72 and 108, which together cover the plane without ever repeating. It has local five-fold symmetry, which no periodic tiling can have. The program builds it from Robinson triangles, the halves of the rhombi. It starts with ten thin triangles arranged round the centre in a decagon, then repeatedly deflates every triangle into smaller ones. A thin triangle becomes two (one of each kind) and a thick one becomes three, with the new vertices dividing the old edges in the golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2.

Each deflation shrinks the edges by 1/φ and multiplies the number of triangles by φ² ≈ 2.618, the larger eigenvalue of the substitution matrix. The subdivisions slider sets how many rounds are made. For colour, each triangle looks up the picture at its centroid. In picture mode the thick tiles are made 4% lighter and the thin ones 6% darker, so the two shapes can be told apart; in duo mode they take gold and teal, shaded by the picture’s tone; in mixed mode the picture colour and the duo colour are mixed 60:40. Optional lines trace the triangles’ outer edges.
